subject: science
title: Understand reversible and irreversible changes
promise: This starts from the one question that sorts every change in this topic: can you get the original material BACK? Melting says yes; burning says no — and everything else follows from telling those two families apart.

sections.heading: The sorting question: can you get it back?
sections.body:
Every change a material goes through belongs to one of two families.
A REVERSIBLE change can be undone — the original material is still there, just in a different state or mixed in. Melt ice and you can refreeze it; dissolve salt and you can get it back.
An IRREVERSIBLE change makes NEW material, and no amount of cooling, drying or waiting brings the old one back. Burn paper and the ash, smoke and gases cannot be turned into paper again.
Before anything else in this topic, ask the sorting question: could I get the original back?
sections.example: Melting chocolate — reversible, cool it and it sets. Baking a cake — irreversible, you cannot un-bake it into eggs and flour.

sections.heading: Dissolving: hidden, not gone
sections.body:
Stir salt into water and it vanishes — but it is NOT gone. It has DISSOLVED: its tiny pieces have spread evenly through the water, far too small to see. The mixture is called a SOLUTION, and the taste proves the salt is still in there.
The evidence that nothing was destroyed: weigh the water, weigh the salt, then weigh the solution — it equals both together. Dissolving hides material; it never deletes it.
Substances that dissolve, like salt and sugar, are called SOLUBLE. Sand is INSOLUBLE — stir all day and it just sinks.
sections.example: 20 g of salt stirred into 200 g of water makes exactly 220 g of salty solution.

sections.heading: Getting it back: separating mixtures
sections.body:
Because mixing and dissolving are reversible, there is a tool for undoing each one — and the right tool depends on the mixture.
A SIEVE separates big pieces from small ones: pasta from water, stones from sand.
A FILTER catches insoluble bits while liquid passes through: sand out of water, the way a coffee filter holds back the grounds.
EVAPORATION recovers a DISSOLVED solid: filter paper cannot catch dissolved salt — it slips through with the water — so instead let the water evaporate away, and the salt is left behind.
Magnets add one more: they pull iron and steel out of a mixture nothing else could sort.
sections.example: Salty water: filtering does nothing, but leave it in a warm dish and the water evaporates, leaving salt crystals.

sections.heading: Irreversible changes make new materials
sections.body:
Some changes create material that simply was not there before.
BURNING turns wood into ash, smoke and gases. COOKING turns runny egg into firm white — cooling it does not make it runny again. RUSTING slowly turns iron into flaky orange rust, a genuinely different substance. Mixing vinegar with bicarbonate of soda fizzes up a NEW gas (carbon dioxide) that neither ingredient contained.
These are chemical changes: the ingredients' building blocks have rearranged into something new, and the old material no longer exists to be recovered.
sections.example: A struck match cannot be un-struck: the wood's material has become ash and gas.

sections.heading: Spotting an irreversible change
sections.body:
Four clues tell you new material has been made.
A NEW COLOUR that will not wash out — iron's orange rust. A GAS GIVEN OFF — fizzing and bubbles where there was no gas before, like vinegar meeting bicarbonate. HEAT OR LIGHT produced by the change itself — burning gives out both. And a NEW TEXTURE that will not reverse — the crisp toast that will never be soft bread again.
One clue is a hint; several together are near-certain. And the final test is always the sorting question: nothing you can do will bring the original back.
sections.example: The cake in the oven browns, rises, firms up and smells different — four signs of new material being made.

mistakes.wrong: Saying dissolved salt has "disappeared" or become part of the water.
mistakes.right: It is still salt, spread through the water in pieces too small to see — evaporate the water and the salt returns.
mistakes.why: The solution weighs the water plus the salt, and tastes of it: hidden is not gone.

mistakes.wrong: Trying to FILTER dissolved salt out of salty water.
mistakes.right: Dissolved material passes through filter paper with the water — use EVAPORATION to recover it.
mistakes.why: A filter catches pieces big enough to trap. Dissolved pieces are far smaller than the paper's holes.

mistakes.wrong: Calling melting an irreversible change because the ice cube is "gone".
mistakes.right: Melting is reversible — the water is the same substance, and freezing brings the ice straight back.
mistakes.why: The sorting question is about getting the MATERIAL back, not the shape. The water was never anything but water.

check.question: Which of these changes is REVERSIBLE?
check.explanation: Cool the melted chocolate and it sets again — same substance throughout. The other three make new materials.

check.question: Salt is stirred into water and vanishes. What has happened?
options: It dissolved — it is spread through the water in pieces too small to see
check.answer: It dissolved — it is spread through the water in pieces too small to see
check.explanation: The salt is hidden, not gone: the solution tastes salty and weighs water plus salt.

check.question: 20 g of sugar dissolves in 100 g of water. What does the solution weigh?
check.explanation: Dissolving hides material but never deletes it — the mass of both together is all still there.

check.question: How do you get dissolved salt back OUT of salty water?
check.explanation: Dissolved salt slips through filters and sieves — but when the water evaporates, the salt is left behind.

check.question: Which tool separates SAND from water?
check.explanation: Sand is insoluble — its grains are big enough for filter paper to catch while the water runs through.

check.question: Which of these is an IRREVERSIBLE change?
check.explanation: Burning makes ash, smoke and gases — new materials that cannot be turned back into wood.

check.question: Vinegar and bicarbonate of soda fizz when mixed. What does the fizzing show?
options: A new gas is being made — an irreversible change
check.answer: A new gas is being made — an irreversible change
check.explanation: The bubbles are carbon dioxide, a substance neither ingredient contained — new material means irreversible.

check.question: What is rust?
options: A new substance made slowly from iron
check.answer: A new substance made slowly from iron
check.explanation: Rusting is a slow chemical change — the orange flakes are a genuinely different material from the iron.

check.question: Which substance is INSOLUBLE in water?
check.explanation: Stir sand all day and it sinks unchanged — unlike salt and sugar, it does not dissolve.

check.question: Which is a reliable SIGN of an irreversible change?
options: A new material appears that cannot be turned back
The substance gets colder in the fridge
check.answer: A new material appears that cannot be turned back
check.explanation: Shape, temperature and mixing can all be undone — new material that resists every undoing is the mark of an irreversible change.

practice.prompt: Is freezing water reversible or irreversible?
practice.answer: Reversible — melt the ice and the same water is back.
practice.hint: Ask the sorting question: can you get the original back?

practice.prompt: Is frying an egg reversible or irreversible?
practice.answer: Irreversible — the firm white is new material, and cooling never makes it runny again.
practice.hint: Can any amount of cooling undo it?

practice.prompt: What do we call a mixture of a dissolved solid and water?
practice.hint: Salt plus water makes a salty ___.

practice.prompt: Name one substance that dissolves in water and one that does not.
practice.answer: Salt (or sugar) dissolves; sand (or flour, chalk) does not.
practice.hint: Soluble and insoluble — one of each.

practice.prompt: You have a mixture of sand and water. How do you separate it, and why does that tool work?
practice.answer: Filter it — sand grains are too big to pass through the filter paper, so the water runs through and the sand stays behind.
practice.hint: The sand never dissolved, so its pieces are still big.

practice.prompt: You have salty water. Why will a filter NOT get the salt back, and what will?
practice.answer: Dissolved salt is in pieces far smaller than the filter's holes, so it passes through with the water. Evaporating the water leaves the salt behind.
practice.hint: One tool catches pieces; the other removes the water instead.

practice.prompt: How could you separate a mixture of iron filings and sand?
practice.answer: Use a magnet — it pulls out the iron and leaves the sand.
practice.hint: One of the two materials is magnetic.

practice.prompt: Give two of the four signs that an irreversible change is happening.
practice.answer: Any two of: a lasting new colour, a gas given off (fizzing), heat or light produced, a new texture that will not reverse.
practice.hint: Think of what burning and baking both show.

practice.prompt: 15 g of sugar dissolves in 185 g of tea. What does the sweet tea weigh, and what does that prove?
practice.answer: 200 g — dissolving hides the sugar but destroys nothing, so the masses simply add.
practice.hint: Where could any missing grams have gone?

practice.prompt: Baking turns runny cake mixture into firm cake. Give two signs from the oven that new material is being made.
practice.answer: It browns (new colour), rises as gas is made inside, firms into a new texture, and smells different — any two.
practice.hint: Use the four-clue checklist on the oven window.

practice.prompt: A bicycle left in the rain grows orange patches. Name the change, say which family it belongs to, and why.
practice.answer: Rusting — irreversible, because the rust is a new substance made from the iron, and nothing brings the shiny iron back.
practice.hint: Is the orange material still iron?

practice.prompt: Plan the steps to get BOTH the sand AND the salt back from a mixture of sand, salt and water.
practice.answer: Filter first — the sand stays on the paper. Then evaporate the filtered salty water — the salt is left behind as crystals.
practice.hint: Two tools, in the right order: catch the insoluble part, then remove the water.
